extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners (and patent practitioners reviewing written description guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent application's specification adequately demonstrates that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention under 35 U.S.C. 112 (written description). Focuses on claim construction, how to review the specification, and types/quality of disclosure that satisfy the requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction — determine what each claim as a whole covers
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim must be separately analyzed and given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description; consider entire claim including preamble language, transitional phrase, and body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include preamble and transitional phrase weight when construing claims. 'Comprising' is open-ended (covers recited elements alone or combined with unrecited elements). 'Consisting essentially of' occupies a middle ground but for 35 U.S.C. 102/103 searching it will be treated as equivalent to 'comprising' unless the specification clearly defines what materially changes the invention. Applicant bears the burden of showing that additional steps/components are excluded by 'consisting essentially of.' Do not import limitations from the specification into the claims. Absence of definitions for well-established terms/procedures is not a basis for a 35 U.S.C. 112 rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review the entire application for support of each element/step
rubrics_metrics.description: Before deciding whether the written description requirement is satisfied, review claims and the entire specification (including embodiments, figures, and sequence listings) to understand how applicant provides support for each claimed feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the specification from the standpoint of one of ordinary skill in the art at the filing date; determine the field of the invention and the level of skill. There is generally an inverse correlation between level of skill in the art and the specificity of disclosure necessary. Use teachings in the specification to assess whether each claim limitation is supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description shows possession by disclosure of an actual reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession may be shown by describing an actual reduction to practice: the inventor constructed an embodiment or performed a process that met all claim limitations and determined the invention would work for its intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction to practice provides strong evidence of possession. For biological materials, a deposit in accordance with 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. may evidence reduction to practice. Case law examples: Cooper v. Goldfarb; UMC Elecs.; Estee Lauder; Mahurkar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description shows possession by drawings or structural/chemical formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear depiction of the invention in detailed drawings or structural chemical formulas that permit one skilled in the art to recognize that applicant had possession can satisfy the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings alone may suffice in some instances. Generic formulas in chemical claims often indicate what the genus encompasses and can be adequate. Cases: Vas-Cath; In re Wolfensperger; Autogiro; Eli Lilly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description shows possession by identifying characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of sufficiently detailed, relevant identifying characteristics (e.g., sequence, structure, binding affinity, binding specificity, molecular weight, length) can demonstrate possession of a claimed biological or chemical entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying characteristics may include partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics coupled with known correlations between function and structure, restriction enzyme maps, unique cleavage patterns, isoelectric points, antibody cross-reactivity, or expression of mRNA producing the protein. The characteristics must distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and lead one skilled in the art to conclude applicant had possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claiming alone is generally insufficient for certain claims (e.g., coding sequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: A functional definition by itself does not suffice to describe a coding sequence or other molecular structures because it indicates what the gene does rather than what it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For chemical inventions, precise definition by structure, formula, chemical name, or physical properties is required; simply providing assays or a plan for identifying active compounds is not enough. Case examples: Eli Lilly; Univ. of Rochester v. G.D. Searle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph) support requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 6 (means- or step-plus-function), it must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts described in the specification and equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A means-plus-function limitation is adequately described under 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 1 if: (1) the written description links/associates adequately described particular structure/material/acts to the recited function; or (2) it is clear that one skilled in the art would know what structure/material/acts perform the recited function. Consider the disclosure in the summary, detailed description, original claims, abstract, and drawings. Note: a 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 2 rejection cannot stand where there is adequate para.1 description for means-plus-function recitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis for claims drawn to a single embodiment or species
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is limited to a single disclosed embodiment/species, analyze whether the application describes possession of that species by (A) actual reduction to practice, (B) reduction to detailed drawings or structural chemical formulas, or (C) sufficiently detailed identifying characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically: (1) Determine whether the application describes the complete structure (or acts of a process) of the claimed invention as a whole; a complete structure typically satisfies 35 U.S.C. 112, para.1. (2) If the complete structure is not disclosed, determine whether other relevant identifying characteristics suffice to show possession (e.g., when there is a well-established correlation between structure and function, function plus minimal structure may suffice). Functional disclosure alone is insufficient where no correlation exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider when determining whether possession is shown
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination that applicant was in possession is a factual inquiry considering multiple factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics (especially if coupled with a known correlation between function and structure), and the method of making the claimed invention. Disclosure of any combination of such identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and would lead one of skill in the art to conclude possession is sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust disclosure expectations to the nature and predictability of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount and type of description necessary under 35 U.S.C. 112 varies with the nature and scope of the invention and with the existing scientific and technological knowledge in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In mature, predictable arts (e.g., well-known microprocessor programming), disclosure of function and a capable device may suffice. In emerging or unpredictable technologies, or where traits are not reasonably predictable, more detailed disclosure (e.g., structure, examples, testing) is required. Disclosure of only a method of making and function may not support a product claim in unpredictable arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claim support
rubrics_metrics.description: A product-by-process claim's written description requirement is satisfied if the process has actually been used to produce the product; otherwise, the requirement may not be met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it is unclear that the acts in the specification can be performed or that the product is produced by the claimed process, written description support for a product-by-process claim may be insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional/art-known subject matter need not be disclosed in detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Information that is conventional or well known to one of ordinary skill in the art need not be described in detail in the specification to satisfy the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on patents and printed publications in the art to determine maturity and the level of knowledge/skill in the art. In mature technologies, a written description question generally should not be raised for claims present in the application when originally filed even if the specification discloses only method and function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim as a whole must be supported including preamble and transitional phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim as a whole — preamble, transitional phrase, and body — must be sufficiently supported by the specification to satisfy the written description requirement; applicant shows possession by describing the claimed invention with all its limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether sufficient structures, acts, or functions are recited to make clear the scope and meaning of the claim, including the weight to be given the preamble. Determination whether preamble recitations are structural limitations requires review of the entire application to understand what the inventors actually invented and intended to encompass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of 'consisting essentially of' transitional phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Consisting essentially of' signals the invention includes listed ingredients and is open to unlisted ingredients that do not materially affect the basic and novel properties; absent clear definition in the specification, treat it as 'comprising' for prior art analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To have a different scope than 'comprising' for 102/103 purposes, the specification should define what constitutes a material change in the basic and novel characteristics. Case example: PPG Industries v. Guardian Industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspective and timing for written description assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether a skilled artisan would have understood the inventor to be in possession of the claimed invention at the time the application was filed; the description need not use the exact words of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inquiry is factual and case-by-case. If a skilled artisan would understand possession despite lack of every nuance in the specification, the requirement is met. Support can be shown even if actual reduction to practice is absent if the disclosure provides sufficient identifying characteristics.
